quizzes.quiz_name: Saqr Academy — AI for Software Development

questions.question_text: What Claude subscription plan does the Setup Guide say is required for this course?
correct_answer: Max ($100/month)
questions.explanation: The Setup Guide lists Claude Max at $100/month as required, since the course relies on the Claude Code feature inside the desktop app.

questions.question_text: What Codex subscription plan does the Setup Guide require?
correct_answer: Plus ($20/month)
questions.explanation: Codex needs at least the Plus plan ($20/month) per the Setup Guide.

questions.question_text: In this course, Claude is the reviewer and Codex is the primary builder.
correct_answer: False
questions.explanation: It's the reverse: Claude is the primary coding partner (the builder, via Claude Code), and Codex is the reviewer and architect.

questions.question_text: Where inside the Claude desktop app do you build apps?
choices: A separate CLI-only tool with no GUI
correct_answer: The Code tab (Claude Code)
questions.explanation: The Setup Guide has you click the Code tab inside the Claude app to reach the Claude Code interface.

questions.question_text: Which command checks whether Git is installed on your computer?
correct_answer: git --version
questions.explanation: `git --version` is the check used on both Mac and Windows in the Setup Guide.

questions.question_text: On a Mac, if Git is missing after the Command Line Developer Tools popup, what command does the guide say to run?
correct_answer: xcode-select --install
questions.explanation: The Mac fallback in the Setup Guide is `xcode-select --install`, run from Terminal.

questions.question_text: On Windows, what command does the guide use to install Git via winget?
correct_answer: winget install Git.Git
questions.explanation: `winget install Git.Git`, run in PowerShell, is the Windows install path in the Setup Guide.

questions.question_text: Which three free-tier accounts does the Setup Guide have you create?
correct_answer: GitHub, Vercel, Supabase
questions.explanation: All three are free and used throughout the program for code hosting, deployment, and databases.

questions.question_text: How does the Setup Guide have you sign up for Vercel and Supabase?
choices: "Continue with GitHub" to link the accounts
A separate email and password for each
By importing a project from GitHub first
correct_answer: "Continue with GitHub" to link the accounts
questions.explanation: Both signups use "Continue with GitHub" so the three accounts are linked from the start.

questions.question_text: What is Vercel used for in this course, per the Setup Guide?
correct_answer: Deploying apps to the internet
questions.explanation: The guide describes Vercel as "how we deploy your apps to the internet."

questions.question_text: What is Supabase used for in this course?
correct_answer: Database and authentication
questions.explanation: The guide calls Supabase "the database and authentication service we use for your apps."

questions.question_text: The Setup Guide's Final Check includes confirming your laptop is charged and ready.
correct_answer: True
questions.explanation: "My laptop is charged and ready for Saturday" is one of the six Final Check items.

questions.question_text: If none of the Git-install fixes work, what does the Setup Guide tell you to do?
choices: Share a screenshot in the group chat
Skip Git and use the browser instead
correct_answer: Share a screenshot in the group chat
questions.explanation: Both the Mac and Windows branches end with the same fallback: share a screenshot in the group chat if the fix doesn't work.

questions.question_text: On Windows, which application does the Setup Guide have you open to check for Git?
correct_answer: PowerShell
questions.explanation: The Windows branch has you press the Windows key, type PowerShell, and open Windows PowerShell.

questions.question_text: What are the four steps of the "build loop" taught in this lesson?
correct_answer: Plan, Build, Verify, Update progress
questions.explanation: The agent proposes a change, edits files, you verify the done condition in the running app, and only then is progress updated.

questions.question_text: In the two-agent model from this lesson, which agent is described as "the builder"?
choices: Neither — the student writes the code
correct_answer: Claude Desktop App
questions.explanation: Claude is the builder; Codex is the reviewer, reading proposed changes before they merge.

questions.question_text: Which agent is described as "the reviewer"?
correct_answer: Codex Desktop App
questions.explanation: Codex acts as the second pair of eyes, reading proposed changes before they merge into the main app.

questions.question_text: What does Row Level Security (RLS) do, per this lesson?
choices: Ensures each user only sees their own data rows
Encrypts the whole database at rest
Limits how many rows a table can hold
Backs up rows automatically every hour
correct_answer: Ensures each user only sees their own data rows
questions.explanation: RLS is the database rule that says "show me only the rows that belong to me" — without it, users could see each other's data.

questions.question_text: Which service hosts the Postgres database used throughout the course?
correct_answer: Supabase
questions.explanation: The lesson names Supabase specifically as the hosted Postgres provider.

questions.question_text: According to this lesson, "shipping" and "releasing" mean the same thing.
correct_answer: False
questions.explanation: Shipping means the code is on the internet; releasing means you can show it to a stranger and stand behind it — a higher bar.

questions.question_text: What are the four release-readiness gates named in this lesson?
choices: Safety, Reliability, UX polish, Demo readiness
correct_answer: Safety, Reliability, UX polish, Demo readiness
questions.explanation: These four gates are laid out in a table, each with its own question the app must pass.

questions.question_text: How is a "Pull Request" defined in the vocabulary card?
choices: A proposal to merge a branch into the main project, opened for review
A request to add a new database column
A ticket asking for a bug fix
A saved checkpoint with a short message
correct_answer: A proposal to merge a branch into the main project, opened for review
questions.explanation: That is the vocabulary card's exact definition of Pull request.

questions.question_text: How is a "Migration" defined in the vocabulary card?
choices: An instruction that updates the database from one schema to the next, safely
Moving a project from Vercel to another host
Copying a repo from GitHub to GitLab
Converting a component from JavaScript to TypeScript
correct_answer: An instruction that updates the database from one schema to the next, safely
questions.explanation: That's the card's definition — the same word used throughout later Supabase-setup prompts in the course.

questions.question_text: What does the vocabulary card say an "Environment variable" is?
choices: A setting or secret kept outside your code so it doesn't leak
A variable whose value changes at runtime
A command-line flag passed to a script
correct_answer: A setting or secret kept outside your code so it doesn't leak
questions.explanation: This is the card's definition, directly relevant to how API keys and Supabase URLs are handled later in the course.

questions.question_text: Roughly how much text does the vocabulary card say one "token" represents?
correct_answer: About ¾ of a word
questions.explanation: The card defines a token as roughly ¾ of a word — how AI models count text.

questions.question_text: Which five documents/files does this lesson say make a project "a system, not a chat"?
choices: PRD, Design Style Guide, Feature List, Progress Tracker, AGENTS.md & CLAUDE.md
PRD, Wireframes, Sitemap, Style Guide, Roadmap
Feature List, Bug Tracker, Release Notes, Changelog, Backlog
correct_answer: PRD, Design Style Guide, Feature List, Progress Tracker, AGENTS.md & CLAUDE.md
questions.explanation: These five hold the agent's standards, scope, and progress so anyone can pick up the project and know what to do.

questions.question_text: What is the first of the two rules for building your homework idea list?
correct_answer: Personal beats clever
questions.explanation: The lesson's example: don't try to invent the next Careem, track your own gym sets.

questions.question_text: What is the second rule for the idea list?
correct_answer: Small beats ambitious
questions.explanation: A working app for one specific person beats a half-built app for "everyone."

questions.question_text: How many app ideas should you aim to have on your list before Session 1?
correct_answer: Ten
questions.explanation: The lesson asks students to aim for ten ideas before Session 1, and to keep adding to the list.

questions.question_text: How does the vocabulary card define "Repo"?
choices: A folder of code, tracked by version control
A single file containing all your code
A cloud storage bucket for backups
The live, deployed version of your app
correct_answer: A folder of code, tracked by version control
questions.explanation: The card calls it "your project's filing cabinet."

questions.question_text: What do cohort members build together across Sessions 1 and 2, per this lesson?
choices: A small intro page, then a Kanban board, then a database-backed task app
A single large e-commerce site over both sessions
correct_answer: A small intro page, then a Kanban board, then a database-backed task app
questions.explanation: These are the two sessions' "reps" — small intro page, then a Kanban board with browser memory, then a real database-backed task app with logins.

questions.question_text: How does the vocabulary card define a "Commit"?
choices: A saved checkpoint with a short message describing the change
The final deployed version of an app
A request to merge a branch
A backup of the entire database
correct_answer: A saved checkpoint with a short message describing the change
questions.explanation: That's the exact card definition.

questions.question_text: This lesson says you need to pre-learn JavaScript or SQL before the program starts.
correct_answer: False
questions.explanation: The lesson explicitly says you don't need to pre-learn JavaScript, SQL, or anything else — the agents handle syntax.

questions.question_text: How does the vocabulary card define "Context window"?
choices: How much text the agent can hold in mind at once
The visible area of the code editor
The time limit on a single agent request
The number of files open in a project
correct_answer: How much text the agent can hold in mind at once
questions.explanation: The card compares it to short-term memory.

questions.question_text: How long is the Session 1 live class?
correct_answer: 180 minutes
questions.explanation: The session header states "Session 01 · 180 min · Live."

questions.question_text: What is the name of the small warm-up app built first in Session 1?
correct_answer: Launch Card
questions.explanation: The Launch Card is Build 1 — a small app used to prove the ship cycle before the real build.

questions.question_text: What is the name of the main Kanban app built in Session 1's Build 2?
correct_answer: Founder Sprint Board
questions.explanation: Build 2 is the Founder Sprint Board — the session's real shipped Kanban micro-product.

questions.question_text: Which two CLI tools get installed and verified in Session 1's Block 02?
correct_answer: GitHub CLI and Vercel CLI
questions.explanation: Block 02, "Permission modes & CLI install," gets both GitHub CLI and Vercel CLI ready.

questions.question_text: What comes right after "Build 1 · Launch Card" in Session 1's block map?
correct_answer: "Why constraints matter" (a teaching block)
questions.explanation: Block 04 teaches why bigger prompts don't make better apps, before Build 2 starts.

questions.question_text: The Founder Sprint Board is built with an open-ended feature list to encourage creativity.
correct_answer: False
questions.explanation: It is built under hard constraints — the whole point of the block is that constrained scope ships better than an open brief.

questions.question_text: What is the exact one-line correction prompt used if Claude adds content outside the Launch Card brief?
choices: "Remove the extra sections. Keep only the Launch Card content from the original brief."
"No. Keep the app inside the original five-feature scope."
"Stop. This is out of scope for today."
"Undo the last change and try again."
correct_answer: "Remove the extra sections. Keep only the Launch Card content from the original brief."
questions.explanation: This is the exact "Scope correction" prompt used for the Launch Card build.

questions.question_text: Which two prompts are reused for both Build 1 and Build 2 to ship the finished app?
choices: Deploy · Vercel CLI and GitHub · CLI
Design improvement and Group chat share
Scope correction and Deploy · Vercel CLI
correct_answer: Deploy · Vercel CLI and GitHub · CLI
questions.explanation: Both builds use a Vercel-deploy prompt and a GitHub-CLI push prompt with the same labels.

questions.question_text: What does the "Group chat share" prompt at the end of Session 1 produce?
choices: A submission template with the live URL and repo for the Founder Sprint Board
A private message to the instructor only
A GitHub issue describing bugs found
correct_answer: A submission template with the live URL and repo for the Founder Sprint Board
questions.explanation: Students post proof of the Founder Sprint Board build to the group chat using this template.

questions.question_text: According to the session's opening, what is the main sentence students should leave thinking?
choices: "I built and shipped a working product today. I can do this."
"I understand every line of code that was written."
correct_answer: "I built and shipped a working product today. I can do this."
questions.explanation: This is the session's closing confidence-building line.

questions.question_text: Which of these is one of the seven things students "leave with" after Session 1?
choices: Direct Claude to deploy the app through Vercel CLI
Write raw SQL migrations by hand
Configure Row Level Security policies manually
Set up a CI/CD pipeline from scratch
correct_answer: Direct Claude to deploy the app through Vercel CLI
questions.explanation: This is listed among the seven capabilities students leave Session 1 with — deployment is agent-directed, not hand-coded.

questions.question_text: What follow-up prompt is used after the Founder Sprint Board is built, if its design looks generic?
correct_answer: Design improvement
questions.explanation: The "Design improvement" prompt asks Claude to improve visual design without changing functionality.

questions.question_text: Session 1's "Class setup · Agent-first" prompt is used at the very start of the session, before any building begins.
correct_answer: True
questions.explanation: It's part of Block 02, getting permission modes and CLI tools ready before Build 1 starts.

questions.question_text: How long is Build 2 (Founder Sprint Board) allotted in Session 1's block map?
correct_answer: 80 minutes
questions.explanation: Build 2 is the largest block of the session, at 80 minutes.

questions.question_text: What is the homework app in Session 1 Homework called?
correct_answer: Client Pipeline Board
questions.explanation: "Second Launch. Build a Pipeline Board" has students build the Client Pipeline Board, a pipeline variant of the class Kanban pattern.

questions.question_text: What is the exact one-line rejection sentence for the Client Pipeline Board homework?
choices: "No. Keep the app inside the original five-feature scope."
"No. Keep this homework inside the approved list only."
correct_answer: "No. Keep the app inside the original five-feature scope."
questions.explanation: This is the exact "Rejection sentence" prompt for the Client Pipeline Board homework.

questions.question_text: How many required features does the Client Pipeline Board have?
correct_answer: Five
questions.explanation: The homework is scoped to exactly five required features, same discipline as the class build.

questions.question_text: What are the four pipeline columns used in the Client Pipeline Board?
correct_answer: Leads, Contacted, Proposal, Won
questions.explanation: These are the four pipeline stages used for the six preloaded client opportunities.

questions.question_text: How many preloaded client opportunities does the Client Pipeline Board start with?
correct_answer: Six
questions.explanation: The feature list requires six preloaded client opportunities spread across the pipeline columns.

questions.question_text: The Client Pipeline Board homework is allowed to include a login and database.
correct_answer: False
questions.explanation: Login and database are explicitly on the "must not include" list for this homework — it saves state locally instead.

questions.question_text: What must the app do when the user reloads the page, per the Save board state feature?
choices: Remember moved and added cards from localStorage
Reset to the six demo opportunities every time
Prompt the user to sign in again
correct_answer: Remember moved and added cards from localStorage
questions.explanation: The board must persist state locally and include a reset button that restores the six demo opportunities.

questions.question_text: Which stretch option involves showing the sum of all opportunity values at the top of the board?
choices: Option C: Add a Lost column
There is no such stretch option
correct_answer: Option A: Total pipeline value
questions.explanation: Three stretch options exist; only one may be added, and only after the required work passes.

questions.question_text: How many stretch features are students allowed to add to the Client Pipeline Board homework?
choices: Exactly one, and only after required work passes
Two, chosen from the three options
None — stretch options are for reference only
correct_answer: Exactly one, and only after required work passes
questions.explanation: The rule is explicit: add only one, and only after the submitted app passes every required check.

questions.question_text: What deliverable format does the homework ask students to submit in the group chat?
choices: Live URL, GitHub repo, and a short reflection template
A pull request link with no other context
correct_answer: Live URL, GitHub repo, and a short reflection template
questions.explanation: The submission template asks for the live URL, repo, the five features shipped, and a scope-control reflection.

questions.question_text: What is the fallback move mechanism required alongside drag-and-drop for moving opportunities?
correct_answer: Move left / Move right buttons
questions.explanation: Simple move buttons are required as a fallback in case drag-and-drop is awkward on trackpad or mobile.

questions.question_text: What does the homework say about installing drag-and-drop npm packages?
choices: Not allowed — use native browser drag-and-drop instead
Only allowed for the stretch feature
correct_answer: Not allowed — use native browser drag-and-drop instead
questions.explanation: "Drag-and-drop package installs" is on the forbidden list — native browser drag-and-drop plus move buttons is required.

questions.question_text: What two command-line tools does this pre-work lesson have students install?
correct_answer: GitHub CLI and Vercel CLI
questions.explanation: The lesson is titled "Command-line tools" and focuses specifically on these two installs.

questions.question_text: Roughly how long does the lesson say this pre-work should take?
correct_answer: Fifteen minutes
questions.explanation: The lesson's framing is "Fifteen minutes. Most of it is waiting for the downloads."

questions.question_text: Which prerequisite technology must be installed before the Vercel CLI, since Vercel CLI ships as an npm package?
correct_answer: Node.js
questions.explanation: The lesson checks `node --version` first, noting most students already have it from Session 1.

questions.question_text: Is installing the Supabase CLI part of this lesson's required setup?
choices: No — it's explicitly listed as not required
Yes, it's the third required tool
Yes, but only for Mac users
correct_answer: No — it's explicitly listed as not required
questions.explanation: The lesson has a "What you are not installing" section: Supabase is controlled from its web dashboard instead.

questions.question_text: Which command verifies you are signed in to GitHub CLI?
correct_answer: gh auth status
questions.explanation: `gh auth status` is the verify step for GitHub CLI in this lesson.

questions.question_text: Which command verifies you are signed in to Vercel CLI?
correct_answer: vercel whoami
questions.explanation: `vercel whoami` returning your username is the verify step for Vercel CLI.

questions.question_text: How does the lesson describe signing in with GitHub CLI?
choices: Choose GitHub.com, then HTTPS, then log in with a web browser
Paste a personal access token directly
Use SSH keys generated in Terminal
Sign in with your email and password
correct_answer: Choose GitHub.com, then HTTPS, then log in with a web browser
questions.explanation: `gh auth login` walks through this exact flow, opening a browser tab for a one-time code.

questions.question_text: How does the lesson have students sign in with Vercel CLI?
choices: Paste an API token from the dashboard
correct_answer: Select "Continue with GitHub"
questions.explanation: `vercel login` has the student select Continue with GitHub, matching the account-linking pattern from Session 1's Setup Guide.

questions.question_text: What is the final checklist item about, beyond the two CLI tools?
choices: Having watched the Session 2 pre-work video and done the database interactive artifact
Bringing a printed copy of the syllabus
correct_answer: Having watched the Session 2 pre-work video and done the database interactive artifact
questions.explanation: This is the fourth checklist item alongside Node, GitHub CLI, and Vercel CLI confirmation.

questions.question_text: What should you do if `node --version` returns "command not found"?
choices: Install the LTS version from nodejs.org and open a new terminal
Ignore it — Node isn't actually needed
Use `npm install node` to fix it
correct_answer: Install the LTS version from nodejs.org and open a new terminal
questions.explanation: The lesson points to the nodejs.org download link and specifies picking the LTS version.

questions.question_text: Why does the lesson say it's worth doing this setup ahead of class rather than during it?
choices: So the Session 2 build ("Build 3") runs without interruption
Because CLI tools can only be installed on weekdays
Because Vercel requires a 24-hour waiting period
Because GitHub CLI needs manual approval from staff
correct_answer: So the Session 2 build ("Build 3") runs without interruption
questions.explanation: The lesson notes Claude Code can sometimes install these tools on the fly, but each still needs a one-time human sign-in — doing that ahead of time avoids interruptions.

questions.question_text: What is the class app built in Session 2 called?
correct_answer: Cloud Task Board
questions.explanation: Session 2 rebuilds the Session 1 board pattern with a database, auth, and RLS as "Cloud Task Board."

questions.question_text: How many project-operating-system documents does Block 03 have Claude scaffold?
correct_answer: Six
questions.explanation: PRD, Design Style Guide, Feature List JSON, Progress Tracker, CLAUDE.md, and CLAUDE.md — six documents, listed as "Doc 01" through "Doc 06."

questions.question_text: What are the four required product features of Cloud Task Board?
choices: Login/logout, database-backed board, move tasks, add/delete tasks
correct_answer: Login/logout, database-backed board, move tasks, add/delete tasks
questions.explanation: These four features (S2-F1 through S2-F4) make up the whole feature list for Cloud Task Board.

questions.question_text: How many mini-sprints does Session 2 run to build the four Cloud Task Board features?
correct_answer: Four
questions.explanation: One sprint per feature, each following the same Plan → Review → Build → Verify → Update tracking rhythm.

questions.question_text: What database columns does the tasks table need per the Supabase setup prompt?
choices: id, user_id, title, status, priority, created_at
correct_answer: id, user_id, title, status, priority, created_at
questions.explanation: This is the exact column list from the Supabase setup prompt for the tasks table.

questions.question_text: What key does the setup prompt say the app should never ask for or use?
correct_answer: The Supabase secret key (service_role)
questions.explanation: "Never ask for or use the Supabase secret key" appears repeatedly across the Session 2 prompts.

questions.question_text: What is the fallback path if the Supabase CLI setup is blocked?
choices: A generated SQL script pasted into the Supabase dashboard SQL Editor
Skip the database and use localStorage instead
Ask an instructor to set it up manually
correct_answer: A generated SQL script pasted into the Supabase dashboard SQL Editor
questions.explanation: Claude generates one complete SQL script and tells the student exactly where to paste it if CLI setup fails.

questions.question_text: What does the "hard rule" of the mini-sprint protocol say about the `passes` flag?
choices: Do not set passes to true unless done_when is actually satisfied
Always set passes to true after building
passes should never change once set
passes is optional and can be skipped
correct_answer: Do not set passes to true unless done_when is actually satisfied
questions.explanation: This rule protects the feature list from becoming an unreliable record of what's actually done.

questions.question_text: What issue does the "Unblock · Email confirmation" prompt address?
choices: Supabase email confirmation blocking test login
A missing environment variable on production
correct_answer: Supabase email confirmation blocking test login
questions.explanation: This prompt asks for the fastest safe development-only way to disable email confirmation when it's blocking test sign-in.

questions.question_text: In Sprint 3 (Move tasks), what two interaction methods must both be supported?
choices: Native drag-and-drop and fallback move buttons
correct_answer: Native drag-and-drop and fallback move buttons
questions.explanation: Same pattern as Session 1: drag-and-drop plus simple move-left/move-right buttons, with no drag-and-drop libraries installed.

questions.question_text: What does RLS specifically enforce on the tasks table in this lesson?
choices: Authenticated users can select, insert, update, and delete only their own rows
Only admins can read the table
All users can see all tasks but not edit them
correct_answer: Authenticated users can select, insert, update, and delete only their own rows
questions.explanation: This is the exact RLS policy scope requested in the Supabase setup prompt.

questions.question_text: What is Session 2's homework app called?
correct_answer: Cloud Pipeline Board
questions.explanation: The homework preview at the end of class points to "Cloud Pipeline Board" as the next build.

questions.question_text: Which environment variable file must stay out of GitHub, per this lesson?
correct_answer: .env.local
questions.explanation: Sprint 1's build prompt repeatedly emphasizes keeping .env.local out of GitHub while using it locally.

questions.question_text: What does Block 04's readiness report check before any building starts?
choices: Git, Node, GitHub CLI, Vercel CLI, and Supabase CLI are all ready
Only whether Supabase is signed up
Whether the student has read the PRD
Whether the Vercel project is already deployed
correct_answer: Git, Node, GitHub CLI, Vercel CLI, and Supabase CLI are all ready
questions.explanation: Block 02, "Tool check," confirms all five before any project or deploy work happens.

questions.question_text: What must happen to environment variables before the production Vercel deploy?
choices: They must be added to Vercel before the production deploy
They only need to exist locally
Vercel generates them automatically at build time
correct_answer: They must be added to Vercel before the production deploy
questions.explanation: The deploy prompt explicitly checks that the required Supabase environment variables are added to Vercel first.

questions.question_text: What new file, introduced in Session 2, specifies each screen's single job and one primary action?
correct_answer: docs/05_Design.md (the Screen Spec)
questions.explanation: This is Doc 06, described as fixing the worst habit of AI-built apps: cluttered screens with competing buttons.

questions.question_text: What is the homework app in Session 2 Homework called?
correct_answer: Cloud Pipeline Board
questions.explanation: Same shape as class (Cloud Task Board) but a sales-pipeline domain, built database-backed with Supabase.

questions.question_text: What table name replaces "tasks" in the Cloud Pipeline Board's database schema?
correct_answer: opportunities
questions.explanation: The Supabase setup prompt creates a public.opportunities table instead of public.tasks.

questions.question_text: What are the four pipeline stages used for opportunities in this homework?
correct_answer: leads, contacted, proposal, won
questions.explanation: These are the exact allowed values for the stage column, matching the Session 1 pipeline naming.

questions.question_text: What is the operating principle repeated throughout this homework about who runs the setup commands?
choices: Claude does the setup; the student authorises
The student runs all CLI commands manually
The instructor sets up Supabase for every student
Setup is skipped and only the app is built
correct_answer: Claude does the setup; the student authorises
questions.explanation: "If the agent can carry out a task, you should not be asked to do it manually" is stated as the operating principle.

questions.question_text: What are the two guardrail files students create before any app code, per Step 02?
correct_answer: CLAUDE.md and features.json
questions.explanation: These two files keep Claude inside the brief before any code is written, with their exact content supplied in the lesson.

questions.question_text: How many opportunities does the reference seed list contain?
correct_answer: Six
questions.explanation: Six starter opportunities are seeded, matching the pattern from the Session 1 homework's Client Pipeline Board.

questions.question_text: Is manually writing database SQL the default path in this homework?
choices: No — Supabase CLI is the default; SQL paste is fallback only
Yes — SQL is always written by hand first
Yes, but only for the opportunities table
correct_answer: No — Supabase CLI is the default; SQL paste is fallback only
questions.explanation: The lesson states this explicitly under "Operating principle": SQL paste in the dashboard is fallback only.

questions.question_text: Roughly what time budget does this homework's Time guidance table suggest overall?
correct_answer: 3.5 to 5 hours
questions.explanation: This is the total in the homework's own time-guidance table, spanning setup through deploy and push.

questions.question_text: What does the homework's "20-minute rule" ask students to do?
choices: Post a screenshot in the group chat if stuck on the same issue for over 20 minutes
Limit each Claude prompt to 20 minutes of runtime
correct_answer: Post a screenshot in the group chat if stuck on the same issue for over 20 minutes
questions.explanation: This rule appears consistently across the course's homework lessons to prevent silent, prolonged struggling.

questions.question_text: What is the last section of this homework, previewing what comes after?
choices: "Prepare for Session 3" — a one-sentence capstone app idea
"Take a break" with no further instructions
A request to grade a classmate's submission
correct_answer: "Prepare for Session 3" — a one-sentence capstone app idea
questions.explanation: Students fill in a template sentence describing the app they want to build for their own Session 3 capstone.

questions.question_text: What must never appear in client-side code, according to this homework's database rule?
correct_answer: The Supabase secret key
questions.explanation: Repeated across the Session 2 track: never ask for or use the Supabase secret key.

questions.question_text: What GitHub CLI action does the homework's push prompt request, alongside committing?
choices: Create the GitHub repo and push it using GitHub CLI
Open a pull request against the Session 1 repo
correct_answer: Create the GitHub repo and push it using GitHub CLI
questions.explanation: Claude is directed to initialize Git if needed, create the repo via GitHub CLI, commit, and push.

questions.question_text: What is this lesson's on-page title?
correct_answer: Give Every Agent a System
questions.explanation: The syllabus nav label is "Agent System Prompts," but the page's own title is "Give Every Agent a System."

questions.question_text: What is the key difference between global and local instruction files, per this lesson?
choices: Global = your default agreements across every project; local = one project's rules
Global applies only to Claude; local applies only to Codex
Global is optional; local is mandatory
correct_answer: Global = your default agreements across every project; local = one project's rules

questions.question_text: What is Claude's global instruction file path, per this lesson?

correct_answer: ~/.codex/AGENTS.md

questions.question_text: How does this lesson say Claude connects to a project's AGENTS.md file?

Claude renames AGENTS.md to CLAUDE.md automatically
Claude and Codex share one merged file

questions.question_text: Why does this lesson say instruction files should be kept thin?
choices: Claude loads CLAUDE.md into context on every turn, burning tokens if it's bloated
Thin files load faster over slow internet
GitHub has a file-size limit for markdown
Thin files are required by the Codex CLI
correct_answer: Claude loads CLAUDE.md into context on every turn, burning tokens if it's bloated
questions.explanation: The lesson's exact reasoning: a huge file means burning tokens on repeated instructions instead of useful work.

questions.question_text: What three control surfaces from Session 2 does this lesson highlight as the agent's real "memory"?
choices: PRD.md, Design Style Guide, Data Model
AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md, and the Screen Spec
correct_answer: CLAUDE.md, docs/04_Feature_List.json, docs/process/progress.md
questions.explanation: These tell the agent what the project is, what's in/out of scope, what's passed, and what's next.

questions.question_text: In this lesson's job-to-tool table, what is recommended for "Reviewing a plan or a PR"?
choices: The other tool, in a fresh thread
The same tool that built it, in the same thread
Always Claude, regardless of who built it
correct_answer: The other tool, in a fresh thread
questions.explanation: The one rule that doesn't change: never let the agent that wrote the code be the only one to review it.

questions.question_text: What does this lesson say to do when stuck on the same failure three times?
choices: Switch model or switch tool — do not keep grinding
Restart the entire project from scratch
Escalate immediately to a human developer
correct_answer: Switch model or switch tool — do not keep grinding
questions.explanation: This is the lesson's exact guidance in its job-to-tool table.

questions.question_text: What does this lesson say a branch is, in the professional workflow it previews?
choices: A safe place to build one feature
A backup of the entire repository
A copy of the production database
correct_answer: A safe place to build one feature
questions.explanation: A pull request is then "the review room for that feature," and a review is where another agent checks the work.

questions.question_text: What is the feature workflow sequence given as a reference in this lesson?
choices: Feature list → branch → plan → build → verify → commit → PR → review → merge → deploy
correct_answer: Feature list → branch → plan → build → verify → commit → PR → review → merge → deploy
questions.explanation: This exact sequence is given as a reference block: "Same shape every feature."

Read the lesson more than once
correct_answer: Create AGENTS.md, edit CLAUDE.md, create global instruction files, create branches, or open pull requests
questions.explanation: This is purely a conceptual pre-work lesson; all hands-on work is saved for the live Session 3 class.

questions.question_text: What will Session 3 build on top of, per this lesson's preview?
choices: The same Session 2 app, turned into "Cloud Task Board Pro"
An entirely new app from scratch
correct_answer: The same Session 2 app, turned into "Cloud Task Board Pro"
questions.explanation: Session 3 continues the same app with a few small, controlled product upgrades — the new complexity is the workflow, not the product.

questions.question_text: This lesson has no copy-paste AI prompts, unlike the live-class lessons.
correct_answer: True
questions.explanation: It is purely conceptual reading alongside a video; its two "Reference" blocks are explicitly captioned "you do not paste this."

questions.question_text: What does Session 3 upgrade Cloud Task Board into?
correct_answer: Cloud Task Board Pro
questions.explanation: Session 3 continues the same app with three controlled feature upgrades.

questions.question_text: What are the three Session 3 feature slices, by their IDs?
questions.explanation: Edit task title/priority (S3-F1), priority filter and column counts (S3-F2), and an optional done summary panel (S3-F3).

correct_answer: Edit task title and priority

correct_answer: feature/S3-F1-edit-task-title-priority
questions.explanation: This exact branch name is given in the "Claude · Create branch" prompt.

questions.question_text: What three possible verdicts can Codex return during a plan review?
correct_answer: APPROVE, APPROVE WITH NOTES, BLOCK
questions.explanation: This exact three-way verdict scale is used in the Codex plan-review prompt.

questions.question_text: What four things does the "UX gate" specifically check on a screen, distinct from the architecture review?
choices: One job, one primary action, an obvious next step, nothing smuggled in
Color contrast, font size, spacing, alignment
Load time, bundle size, accessibility score, SEO
Database schema, RLS, API routes, secrets
correct_answer: One job, one primary action, an obvious next step, nothing smuggled in
questions.explanation: The lesson is explicit: "Architecture review and UX review are not the same thing" — this gate checks flow and focus only.

correct_answer: Squash merge
questions.explanation: Every "Merge" prompt in this lesson specifies squash merge, then switching back to and pulling the latest main.

correct_answer: P0 (blocks merge) through P3 (optional polish)

questions.question_text: What is the "hard rule" stated after Sprint 1 in this lesson?
choices: Do not let the same context approve itself — build in one window, review in a separate one
Always merge without review to save time
Review must happen before the plan is approved
correct_answer: Do not let the same context approve itself — build in one window, review in a separate one
questions.explanation: This is stated verbatim as the hard rule closing out Sprint 1.

questions.question_text: What is Sprint 2 in this lesson specifically designed to prove?
choices: That the project rules are portable — either Claude or Codex can build from the same rulebook
That Codex is strictly better than Claude at building
That two agents can edit the same file simultaneously
That branches are unnecessary for small features
correct_answer: That the project rules are portable — either Claude or Codex can build from the same rulebook
questions.explanation: Sprint 2 is called the "Agent switch drill" — Codex builds S3-F2 by default, with Claude as fallback.

questions.question_text: What does AGENTS.md need to include, per the local project rulebook prompt?

Only a list of npm dependencies
Nothing — it can be an empty file

questions.explanation: This is the exact required-contents list from the "Create · Local instruction system" prompt.

correct_answer: @AGENTS.md

choices: AGENTS.md under 80 lines, CLAUDE.md under 45 lines
AGENTS.md under 200 lines, CLAUDE.md under 100 lines
correct_answer: AGENTS.md under 80 lines, CLAUDE.md under 45 lines

A calendar view of due dates
A chart of tasks completed per week

A production deploy of the current app

The Session 2 app must be deleted and rebuilt
correct_answer: A clean baseline commit of just the workflow-setup files

Auto-scoring leads by likelihood to convert

questions.question_text: Where must the LLM API key live, per the hard constraints?
choices: A server-side environment variable, never in client code
Hardcoded in the frontend for simplicity
In the Supabase anon key field
correct_answer: A server-side environment variable, never in client code
questions.explanation: Stated as a hard boundary for S3-H2, and re-checked explicitly during its code review.

correct_answer: docs/05_Design.md, the newly bootstrapped screen spec

questions.question_text: What must a submission for this homework include, per the group chat template?

Only a screenshot of the finished app
A video recording of the whole build process
A written essay about the experience
correct_answer: Live URL, GitHub repo, and two PR links

choices: Any AI feature beyond the single draft-follow-up action
correct_answer: Any AI feature beyond the single draft-follow-up action

Contacts can be deleted by any authenticated user

questions.question_text: What does this lesson say "release-ready" means?
choices: The current version is honest about what it is and isn't
The app has every feature the student can imagine
The app has zero bugs of any kind
The app has been reviewed by a lawyer
correct_answer: The current version is honest about what it is and isn't
questions.explanation: "A release is not a feeling. A release is evidence" — release-ready means checked, documented, and honest about limitations.

questions.question_text: What order does this lesson insist the release gates run in?
choices: Safety, then reliable, then usable, then presentable
Presentable, then usable, then safety, then reliable
All four gates run in parallel with no order
Usable, then safety, then presentable, then reliable
correct_answer: Safety, then reliable, then usable, then presentable
questions.explanation: "If safety fails, no amount of UX polish makes the release ready" — the gates are strictly sequential.

A printed resume, a business card, a laptop charger, a notebook

Nothing — Session 4 starts from a blank slate
correct_answer: The GitHub repo, the Vercel live URL, the project open in Claude Code, Codex available
questions.explanation: These are the exact four items in "Have these four ready."

correct_answer: Add new features, redesign the UI, or try to fix everything alone
questions.explanation: The whole point is to bring the app as-is; the release process happens together in class.

Always rotate every key before Session 4

Rotate keys only if the app has over 100 users
correct_answer: Do not rotate keys unless you already know a secret was leaked

questions.explanation: Safety gate, Reliability gate, UX and design gate, Demo and release gate.

correct_answer: Safety gate
questions.explanation: Secrets, auth protection, RLS policies, and production environment variables checked, blockers fixed or documented.

questions.question_text: What is explicitly forbidden work during Session 4?
choices: New product modules, payment flows, and full redesigns that change product structure
correct_answer: New product modules, payment flows, and full redesigns that change product structure
questions.explanation: Session 4's hard constraints keep the work to safety, reliability, UX polish, and demo readiness — not new features.

Delete the entire repository and start over

questions.question_text: In the safety audit prompt, what should the public Supabase client use?

The service_role key for full access
No key at all — public access is disabled
correct_answer: NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_URL and the publishable/anon key only

An automated linter with no AI involvement

correct_answer: BLOCK and NOTE
questions.explanation: BLOCK = should be fixed before release; NOTE = polish that can wait.

correct_answer: S4_Release_Readiness.md, S4_Demo_Script.md, S4_Release_Notes.md

A peer-graded rubric filled out silently
correct_answer: A six-step demo format ending with an honest limitation or next feature

choices: Revoke or rotate the exposed secret first; history cleanup is a separate decision
Immediately delete the whole GitHub organization
Contact GitHub support before doing anything else
Wait 30 days before rotating the key
correct_answer: Revoke or rotate the exposed secret first; history cleanup is a separate decision

All four gates merged with zero exceptions
Just a working local build, no deployment required
correct_answer: Safety gate completed, production URL works, one workflow demoable, blockers written down
questions.explanation: This is the lesson's own "Minimum acceptable" bar, distinct from the "Strong outcome" of all four gates passing.

questions.question_text: How many blocks make up Session 4's live class?
correct_answer: Eight
questions.explanation: Opening, tool check, release-track setup, four gates, showcase, and close — eight blocks total.

questions.question_text: What recognition categories does the closing block hand out to the cohort?
choices: Strongest workflow discipline, best design improvement, best debugging recovery, clearest demo, strongest persistence, cleanest release evidence
Fastest typer, most lines of code, biggest app
No recognition is given — the course simply ends
correct_answer: Strongest workflow discipline, best design improvement, best debugging recovery, clearest demo, strongest persistence, cleanest release evidence
questions.explanation: Each certificate names a specific behavior that showed up across the cohort, not just the final app.

questions.question_text: This session introduces new database tables as a normal part of the release process.
correct_answer: False

questions.question_text: What is required before students can consider S4-R1 (safety) done?
choices: Secrets, auth, RLS, and env vars checked, with blockers fixed or documented
A perfect security score from an external scanner
Zero findings of any kind from Codex
correct_answer: Secrets, auth, RLS, and env vars checked, with blockers fixed or documented
questions.explanation: "Or documented" is key — a gate can be considered handled even if a blocker remains, as long as it's written down honestly.

questions.question_text: Is there required homework after Session 4?
choices: No — this is a graduate reference, not an assignment
Yes — a peer code review of another student's app
correct_answer: No — this is a graduate reference, not an assignment
questions.explanation: The lesson states clearly: no required homework is assigned after Session 4.

questions.question_text: What is the core message of this graduate page?
choices: The point is not the app you built — it's the delivery system you can repeat
You should immediately start monetizing your Cloud Task Board Pro
The course is not truly finished until you find a job
You must now learn a new programming language from scratch
correct_answer: The point is not the app you built — it's the delivery system you can repeat
questions.explanation: "The point is not that you built Cloud Task Board Pro. The point is that you can repeat the process."

questions.question_text: What is the suggested time budget, or "rule of thumb," for your next solo build?

correct_answer: Eleven

questions.question_text: How many checks are on the solo release checklist?
correct_answer: Ten
questions.explanation: A condensed version of the Session 4 gates, for use before showing an app to anyone.

questions.question_text: Which items does the release checklist include?
choices: .env.local is ignored, and no secret keys are committed
The app has at least 100 active users
The app has a paid subscription tier
correct_answer: .env.local is ignored, and no secret keys are committed
questions.explanation: These are the first two of the ten release-checklist items.

questions.question_text: What six things should you bring when asking for help, per this lesson?

Your resume, a cover letter, and three references
A full video recording of the whole session
Nothing — just describe the problem verbally
correct_answer: Repo link, live URL, branch name, feature ID, error message, what the agent already tried
questions.explanation: This is the exact "Bring six things to the helper" list.

questions.question_text: Which of these is listed as a reason to ask for help rather than fight it alone?
choices: Auth works locally but fails in production
The app's color scheme feels slightly off
You want a second opinion on a variable name
The build takes longer than expected
correct_answer: Auth works locally but fails in production
questions.explanation: This is one of the seven specific "when to ask for help" triggers, alongside leaked secrets and RLS problems.

questions.question_text: What is the "graduate standard" this lesson closes with?
choices: I can direct agents through a controlled delivery process and ship evidence
I know how to prompt an AI model effectively
I have memorized every Git command
I can write code without any AI assistance
correct_answer: I can direct agents through a controlled delivery process and ship evidence
questions.explanation: The lesson explicitly contrasts this with "I know how to prompt" as the lower, insufficient bar.

questions.question_text: How many audit modules does this security lab walk through, in order?
correct_answer: Seven
questions.explanation: Scope, Threat Model, Database Audit, Auth and API, AI Features, Agentic Pen Test, and Fix/Verify/Document.

questions.question_text: What is this lesson's central reframe of what "security" means?
choices: It is not whether the app works, but what it allows when someone tries to break it
It is purely about having an SSL certificate
It is a checkbox exercise done once before launch
It only matters for apps handling payments
correct_answer: It is not whether the app works, but what it allows when someone tries to break it
questions.explanation: This is stated as "THE REFRAME" at the top of the lab.

questions.question_text: According to Module 01, what does "the UI stops them" actually mean as a security answer?
choices: You have built suggestions, not security
It is a valid and sufficient security control
It only applies to mobile apps
correct_answer: You have built suggestions, not security
questions.explanation: "UI restrictions are not security. A hidden button does not mean a closed endpoint."

questions.question_text: For the lightweight CRM specifically, what two surfaces does the lab say to audit hardest?
choices: Contact data isolation, and the AI Draft follow-up feature
The login page's color scheme, and the footer links
The pricing page, and the marketing copy
The 404 error page, and the favicon
correct_answer: Contact data isolation, and the AI Draft follow-up feature
questions.explanation: Can User A reach User B's contacts by changing an ID, and can a planted note steer or leak data through the AI feature?

questions.question_text: What six deliverables does the threat-model prompt ask an agent to return?
choices: Sensitive assets, roles/trust boundaries, external services/secrets, attack surfaces, top 10 abuse cases, highest-risk flows
A finished penetration test report with fixes applied
A rewritten app with security bugs already patched
A cost estimate for hiring a security consultant
correct_answer: Sensitive assets, roles/trust boundaries, external services/secrets, attack surfaces, top 10 abuse cases, highest-risk flows
questions.explanation: The threat-model prompt explicitly says "Do not fix anything yet" — it's a map, not a fix.

questions.question_text: In the Module 03 checkpoint, how do you personally test cross-user data isolation?
choices: Log in as User A, note a record ID, then try to access it as User B in a private window
Read the RLS policy source code only, without running the app
Ask the agent whether RLS is enabled and trust the answer
Check whether the login page requires a password
correct_answer: Log in as User A, note a record ID, then try to access it as User B in a private window
questions.explanation: This hands-on test is explicitly required — reading the policy alone isn't enough.

questions.question_text: Per Module 04, where must ownership checks on user data be enforced?
choices: Server-side, not just in a client-side hook
Only in the React component's useEffect
correct_answer: Server-side, not just in a client-side hook
questions.explanation: "An attacker never touches the client" — client-side-only authorization is explicitly listed as a vulnerability class.

questions.question_text: What five AI-specific abuse categories does Module 05 test for?
choices: Overriding system instructions, extracting hidden prompts, cross-user data leakage via retrieval, unsafe tool calls, cost/background-work abuse
SQL injection, XSS, CSRF, and clickjacking
Slow page load, broken links, missing alt text, poor color contrast
Weak passwords, missing 2FA, session timeout issues
correct_answer: Overriding system instructions, extracting hidden prompts, cross-user data leakage via retrieval, unsafe tool calls, cost/background-work abuse
questions.explanation: These map directly to the five bullet questions under "What you are testing for" in Module 05.

questions.question_text: What environment restriction applies to the Agentic Pen Test in Module 06?
choices: Local or test environment only — never production or a third party
It must run against the live production URL
It requires written permission from a third-party host
It can only be run by a certified security professional
correct_answer: Local or test environment only — never production or a third party
questions.explanation: Stated in bold: "You are attacking yourself, not the internet."

questions.question_text: What severity scale does the Agentic Pen Test checkpoint ask students to assign themselves?
correct_answer: Critical, High, Medium, Low, Informational
questions.explanation: And the checkpoint explicitly says not to trust the agent's own rating without checking it yourself.

questions.question_text: What does Module 07 say most fixes after an audit look like, if done wrong?
choices: Cosmetic — the button gets hidden, the error message gets prettier, the hole stays open
Overly aggressive — the whole feature gets deleted
Too slow — fixes always take longer than the audit itself
Automatic — the agent silently fixes everything without review
correct_answer: Cosmetic — the button gets hidden, the error message gets prettier, the hole stays open
questions.explanation: A real fix must be enforced server-side or at the database layer, not just in the UI.

questions.question_text: What must a real fix be backed by, per Module 07?
choices: A regression test that fails without the fix and passes with it
A signed statement from the original developer
A second, unrelated feature shipped alongside it
correct_answer: A regression test that fails without the fix and passes with it
questions.explanation: This is one of four criteria for "what a real fix looks like."

questions.question_text: Where do most database-layer fix patterns say privileged operations should move?
choices: Into a public API with no auth
correct_answer: Into server-only code paths
questions.explanation: Listed under the "Database" fix-pattern category in the reference material.

questions.question_text: What does the reference material say about signed URLs for storage?
choices: Use them when files should be private, with short expiries
They are unnecessary if RLS is enabled
They should never expire, for convenience
They replace the need for authentication entirely
correct_answer: Use them when files should be private, with short expiries
questions.explanation: This is one of the "Storage" fix-pattern bullets.

questions.question_text: What does the closing principle say you should never claim about your app?
choices: That it has been tested at all
That it was built with AI agents
correct_answer: That it is unhackable
questions.explanation: "Never tell anyone the app is unhackable. Tell them what you tested, what you found, what you fixed, and what is still open."

questions.question_text: What ten sections does the Final Audit Report prompt require?
choices: Scope, auth/authz, Supabase/RLS, API/server-side, AI-specific, secrets/env vars, storage/uploads, fixed today, still open, recommended next actions
Only a pass/fail summary with no detail
A list of every file in the repository
A financial cost-benefit analysis of the fixes
correct_answer: Scope, auth/authz, Supabase/RLS, API/server-side, AI-specific, secrets/env vars, storage/uploads, fixed today, still open, recommended next actions
questions.explanation: This is the exact ten-item structure from the "Prompt · Final audit report" block.
